subject: principles-of-flight
source_policy: Approved POF handbook remains the technical source of truth. No new production visual may advance beyond source/design brief without question-specific technical, teaching and visual QA.

concepts.concept: Steady-climb force components: lift is less than total weight and thrust is greater than drag

source.figure: Figure 1-37 — Forces acting on an airplane in a climb
source.notes: The handbook resolves weight into a component opposing lift and a rearward component along the flight path. In equilibrium, thrust balances drag plus the rearward weight component, while lift balances only the perpendicular component of weight.

brief.student_must_understand: In a steady climb the aircraft is not climbing because lift exceeds weight. Weight is resolved relative to the inclined flight path, so wing lift is less than total weight and thrust must exceed drag.
preserve: Inclined climb flight path
Lift perpendicular to the flight path
Drag opposite the flight path
Thrust along the flight path
Weight vertically downward
Weight components parallel and perpendicular to the flight path
refine: Make the two weight components visually obvious
Separate the force vectors cleanly from the aircraft silhouette
Emphasize T > D and L < W only after the vector geometry is visible
add: Short note that the rearward weight component is what makes the thrust requirement exceed drag
remove: Any claim that excess lift is the cause of climb

concepts.mapping_reason: All six questions test the same exact steady-climb force relationship.

concepts.concept: Best rate of climb Vy occurs where excess power is greatest

source.figure: Figure 1-38 — Power available vs. power required
source.notes: The handbook states that the vertical distance between power-available and power-required curves is excess power and that the best climbing airspeed is where excess power is maximum.

brief.student_must_understand: Vy is the speed that gives the greatest altitude gain per unit time because it occurs at maximum excess power.
preserve: Power available curve
Power required curve
Airspeed horizontal axis
Power vertical axis
Vertical separation between the curves as excess power
refine: Clean and enlarge the two curves
Label the corresponding airspeed as Vy without inventing a numeric speed
add: Greatest height per unit time takeaway

concepts.mapping_reason: Both questions test Vy as the best-rate speed; the visual teaches the exact excess-power relationship that makes Vy the best-rate speed.

concepts.concept: Best angle of climb Vx gives the greatest height gain over the shortest horizontal distance and is used for obstacle clearance

source.notes: The handbook defines Vx as the speed for best angle of climb and explicitly identifies best-angle climb speed as important for a short-field takeoff where an obstacle must be cleared.

brief.student_must_understand: Vx is about height gained per horizontal distance, not height gained per unit time. It produces the steepest ground-referenced climb path for obstacle clearance under the stated conditions.
preserve: Vx = best angle of climb
Obstacle-clearance use case
Horizontal distance as the comparison basis
No numeric Vx value unless aircraft-specific data are provided
refine: Use a clean side-view climb-path comparison
Make the shorter horizontal distance to clear a fixed obstacle visually obvious
Avoid implying that Vx is the best-rate speed
add: Greatest height per shortest horizontal distance takeaway

concepts.mapping_reason: All five questions test the same exact Vx/obstacle-clearance relationship.

concepts.concept: Wind changes glide path over the ground, not the aerodynamic glide angle or air-mass rate of descent at the same optimum glide condition

source.notes: The handbook states that into-wind glide covers less ground distance and appears steeper to a ground observer, while downwind glide covers more ground distance. It explicitly states the actual glide angle through the moving air mass is unchanged and that the rate of descent is the same in both cases.

brief.student_must_understand: A headwind reduces groundspeed, so the aircraft covers less ground for the same height loss and the ground-referenced glide path is steeper. A tailwind does the opposite. The aerodynamic glide through the air mass is unchanged by steady wind.
preserve: Same starting altitude
Same optimum glide condition through the air mass
Headwind = shorter ground distance and steeper observed path
Tailwind = longer ground distance and shallower observed path
Same rate of descent through the air mass
refine: Use a matched side-by-side headwind/tailwind comparison
Hold height loss constant in both panels
Make the ground-distance difference the main visual cue
add: Ground path: steeper vs shallower labels
remove: Any suggestion that steady wind changes L/D
Any suggestion that steady wind directly changes the air-mass rate of descent

concepts.mapping_reason: All three questions test the same exact wind-versus-ground-glide-path relationship.

concepts.concept: A conventional adjustable elevator trim tab keeps its selected angle relative to the elevator; its aerodynamic force then biases the elevator

source.notes: The handbook describes the elevator trim tab as a separately controlled auxiliary surface on the elevator and states that an upward tab deflection forces the elevator downward while a downward tab deflection forces the elevator upward. The selected trim-tab angle is treated relative to the control surface, not as an automatically coupled balance tab.

brief.student_must_understand: A simple trim tab is not a balance tab. Once set, it keeps the selected angle relative to the elevator as the elevator moves; airflow on the tab supplies a force that helps hold the elevator in the trimmed position.
preserve: Trim tab hinged to the elevator trailing edge
Trim tab separately adjustable from the primary elevator control
Selected tab angle shown relative to the elevator
Aerodynamic force on the tab biases the elevator in the opposite direction
refine: Show the tab/elevator relationship in two elevator positions
Keep the selected tab angle relative to the elevator visually constant
Differentiate simple trim-tab behavior from automatically coupled balance-tab behavior
add: Small airflow-force arrow where it helps explain the bias

concepts.mapping_reason: All three questions test the same exact simple trim-tab setting relationship relative to the elevator.
